meta.blurb: Joon-ho Park wakes to static. A solar flare has knocked out his radio, his crew has lifted off without him, and everyone thinks he is gone. He has one sealed base, one weak air filter and one stubborn plan: stay alive.
meta.bible: Joon-ho Park: thirty-eight, an engineer, dry-humoured and practical; the narrator, who writes the log in first person, past or present tense as in the beat. Aster Base: the small lunar base on the rim of Shackleton crater at the Moon's south pole, with a habitat, a lander pad, a ridge to the north, a rover and solar panels. Captain Ivana Ruiz: the mission commander. Lars Berg: the crew's doctor and pilot. Tomas Okoye: the crew's geologist. Dr Imani Adeyemi: the voice of Mission Control on Earth. Min-seo: Joon-ho's sister on Earth. Pelican: the rescue lander. Gateway: the crew's orbiting station. The Moon: low gravity, no air, hot days and cold nights, with the Earth always low in the sky from the pole. The flare: a burst of radiation from the Sun that knocked out the radio. The scrubber: the air filter that removes carbon dioxide; it is renewed by heating and venting to space. The relay: a small radio mast Joon-ho builds on the ridge. The eclipse: when the Earth passes in front of the Sun, seen from the Moon. The cress: a tray of salad seedlings Joon-ho grows. The rescue takes about seventy days. This book is science fiction with realistic details; no invented real people. Voice: first person, honest, funny, tense, hopeful; no gore. Day numbers are written in words.

beats.scene: Joon-ho lies in a small rover shelter on a grey, dusty ridge
beats.summary: Joon-ho wakes in the rover shelter after the flare and hears only static on his radio.

beats.scene: A small rover drives across grey dunes toward an empty landing pad
beats.summary: Joon-ho drives back to Aster Base and finds the landing pad empty, with only boot prints in the dust.

beats.scene: A whiteboard on a metal wall with a handwritten message beside a photo
beats.summary: Joon-ho finds a note on the whiteboard, and realises that his crew thought he was dead.

beats.scene: Joon-ho counts boxes of food and tanks of air in a cramped storeroom
beats.summary: Joon-ho counts the base's food, water, air and power to see how long he can live.

beats.scene: Joon-ho stares at a calendar and a pencilled sum on the whiteboard
beats.summary: Joon-ho works out that a rescue is possible only if Earth learns he is alive, so the radio must be fixed.

beats.scene: A scorched radio dish stands outside the base beneath a black sky
beats.summary: Joon-ho finds the big radio dish scorched by the flare, and it will not work.

beats.scene: Dust sprays from a loose seal near the airlock door
beats.summary: On day three Joon-ho hears a hiss at the airlock, finds dust in a seal, and cleans it carefully.

beats.scene: A red warning light glows on a panel beside a disassembled air filter
beats.summary: On day four the carbon dioxide alarm sounds, and Joon-ho finds that the scrubber's vent valve has broken.

beats.scene: Joon-ho holds a small metal valve under a lamp with tools around him
beats.summary: Joon-ho borrows a spare valve from the broken hydroponics pump, installs it and starts the scrubber again.

beats.scene: Joon-ho raises a mug of tea in front of a panel of green lights
beats.summary: The carbon dioxide falls, and on day six Joon-ho celebrates with a mug of cold tea.

beats.scene: Joon-ho brushes grey dust from long blue solar panels with a pole
beats.summary: On day eight Joon-ho brushes dust from the solar panels with a long pole to get back power.

beats.scene: Joon-ho pins a daily schedule beside a small tray of cress seeds
beats.summary: On day nine Joon-ho makes a daily timetable and plants a tray of cress seeds under a lamp.

beats.scene: Joon-ho studies a dim screen showing the Earth low over a jagged rim
beats.summary: On day ten Joon-ho works out that Earth hangs low behind the crater rim, so a radio needs a high place.

beats.scene: The rover climbs a steep grey slope with solar panels strapped to its roof
beats.summary: On day twelve Joon-ho loads panels and a transmitter and drives the rover carefully up the steep ridge trail.

beats.scene: Earth glows blue and white above a bleak grey horizon
beats.summary: At the top on day thirteen Joon-ho sees the Earth, bright and blue, hanging above the horizon.

beats.scene: Joon-ho bolts a thin mast and two panels onto a rocky ridge
beats.summary: On day fourteen Joon-ho builds a small relay mast with a transmitter and two panels on the ridge.

beats.scene: Joon-ho kneels to adjust the angle of a small antenna pointed at Earth
beats.summary: On day sixteen the first message gets no answer, and Joon-ho realises he must re-aim as the Earth wobbles.

beats.scene: Joon-ho taps a keyboard in the rover cab while a pale Earth shines outside
beats.summary: On day seventeen Joon-ho aims better and repeats his message, but still hears only silence.

beats.scene: Joon-ho sits beside a tray of green seedlings with his chin in his hand
beats.summary: By day nineteen hope is fading, but Joon-ho keeps his routine and talks to the cress seedlings.

beats.scene: Joon-ho scribbles numbers on a screen showing the Earth and the Sun almost touching
beats.summary: On day twenty-one Joon-ho reads the sky tables and finds a coming eclipse that will cut off his sunlight.

beats.scene: Joon-ho wraps blankets around a battery bank and switches off lights
beats.summary: On day twenty-two Joon-ho prepares by turning off every machine he does not need and wrapping himself in blankets.

beats.scene: A black Earth with a thin glowing red ring above a dark ridge
beats.summary: During the eclipse the Earth blacks out the Sun and shines with a thin red ring of light, and Joon-ho is awestruck.

beats.scene: Joon-ho sits wrapped in blankets while the battery light blinks low
beats.summary: The cold creeps in and the batteries run low, but then the Sun returns and the panels revive the base.

beats.scene: Joon-ho leans toward a speaker while a green light blinks
beats.summary: On day twenty-three a voice answers on the radio, and Dr Adeyemi says that Earth hears him.

beats.scene: Joon-ho listens with a hand over his mouth as a screen glows
beats.summary: Dr Adeyemi tells him the plan: a rescue lander called Pelican will launch in about forty days.

beats.scene: Joon-ho hears the crew's voices crackling through the radio
beats.summary: Captain Ruiz, Lars and Tomas speak to him, glad that he is alive, and Lars makes a joke about the tea.

beats.scene: Joon-ho drives a rover that pushes a flat plate across grey ground
beats.summary: On day twenty-six Joon-ho clears a landing area for the Pelican with a plough made from a rover plate.

beats.scene: Joon-ho bangs on a stuck outer airlock door with the dark ridge behind him
beats.summary: On day twenty-eight the outer door of the airlock sticks and Joon-ho is trapped outside with limited air.

beats.scene: Joon-ho pulls a red emergency lever beside the outer airlock door
beats.summary: Joon-ho remembers the manual lever under a cover, pulls it, and the door opens just in time.

beats.scene: Joon-ho writes in a notebook beside a bandaged hand and a cup of tea
beats.summary: On day thirty Joon-ho rests, writes the log, and remembers that surviving is a series of small, careful choices.

beats.scene: Joon-ho hangs his head as a radio message scrolls across a screen
beats.summary: On day thirty-three Mission Control says the Pelican will be ten days late, and Joon-ho takes the news calmly.

beats.scene: Joon-ho holds a pinch of green cress seedlings above a plain cracker
beats.summary: On day thirty-four Joon-ho harvests the cress and eats his first fresh food in a month on a cracker.

beats.scene: Joon-ho listens to a recorded message with his sister's face on a screen
beats.summary: On day thirty-six Joon-ho receives a recorded message from his sister Min-seo and replies with photos.

beats.scene: Joon-ho lifts a rope with bands tied to a bar in the base
beats.summary: On day forty Joon-ho builds an exercise rig from stretchy cords to keep his muscles and bones strong.

beats.scene: Joon-ho holds up a thin strip of paper that bends toward a tiny crack
beats.summary: On day forty-two Joon-ho hears a hiss, finds a tiny leak by watching a paper ribbon, and patches it.

beats.scene: Joon-ho reads a warning on a screen showing a bright Sun
beats.summary: On day forty-four Mission Control warns him of a solar storm, and he must take shelter within a day.

beats.scene: Joon-ho stacks blue water containers into a thick wall around a bunk
beats.summary: On day forty-five Joon-ho builds a shelter from water containers, because water is a good shield against radiation.

beats.scene: Joon-ho sits in a ring of blue containers singing quietly to himself
beats.summary: For two days Joon-ho waits in the shelter, singing and counting the hours until the storm passes.

beats.scene: Joon-ho climbs a dusty trail toward a thin mast on the ridge
beats.summary: On day forty-seven Joon-ho drives to the ridge to check that the relay survived the storm.

beats.scene: Joon-ho kneels with a small tool beside an opened radio box
beats.summary: On day forty-eight Joon-ho finds that the power regulator is burned out and replaces it with a spare.

beats.scene: Joon-ho listens to a radio message while a calendar shows a circled day
beats.summary: On day fifty Mission Control confirms the new launch date, and Joon-ho prepares the pad and a beacon.

beats.scene: Joon-ho writes with a marker beneath the crew's old note on the whiteboard
beats.summary: On day fifty-two Joon-ho writes a reply under the crew's note and thanks them for coming back.

beats.scene: Joon-ho sits cross-legged playing a battered mouth organ
beats.summary: On day fifty-five Joon-ho finds Tomas's forgotten harmonica and plays badly inside the base.

beats.scene: Joon-ho reads messages on a screen from smiling children in a classroom
beats.summary: On day sixty a school class on Earth sends messages, and a girl asks if he is scared, and he answers honestly.

beats.scene: Joon-ho packs a small bag of rock samples and a jar of seeds
beats.summary: On day sixty-three Joon-ho does his final checks, packs the crew's samples and keeps some cress seeds.

beats.scene: Joon-ho watches a screen with the Pelican leaving a bright orbiting station
beats.summary: On day sixty-eight the Pelican leaves Gateway with Captain Ruiz and Lars, and Joon-ho watches the screen.

beats.scene: Joon-ho stands at a window as a lander descends on a plume of dust
beats.summary: On day seventy-one the Pelican descends over the landing site, throwing dust in a wide arc.

beats.scene: Joon-ho in a spacesuit hugs two crew members at an open lander hatch
beats.summary: On day seventy-two the hatch opens, and Joon-ho hugs Captain Ruiz and Lars for a long time.

beats.scene: Joon-ho writes a last line on the whiteboard in the empty base
beats.summary: Before leaving, Joon-ho writes a last note on the whiteboard for the next visitor and takes his cress seeds.

beats.scene: The Pelican rises from the grey surface toward a small blue Earth
beats.summary: On day seventy-three the Pelican lifts off, and Joon-ho watches the Earth grow larger and ends his log.

A1A2: Day one: I wake up alone, and the radio only makes a hissing noise.
I drive to the base, and the landing pad is empty.
On the board I read a note from my crew.
I count the food, the water, the air and the power.
I know that Earth must learn I am alive, so I must fix the radio.
Day two: The big radio dish is burned and broken.
On day three, the door makes a hissing sound, and I find dust in it.
On day four, an alarm sounds, and the air filter has a problem.
I take a spare valve from another machine and fix the filter.
On day six, the air is clean again, and I drink tea.
On day eight, I clean dust from the solar panels with a long brush.
On day nine, I make a plan for each day and plant small green seeds.
On day ten, I plan to put a radio on the high ridge.
On day twelve, I load the rover and drive up the ridge.
On day thirteen, at the top, I see the Earth, and it is blue.
On day fourteen, I build a small radio mast on the ridge.
On day sixteen, I send my first message, but no one answers.
On day seventeen, I aim better, but I hear only silence.
On day nineteen, I am sad, but I talk to my little plants.
On day twenty-one, I see that the Earth will block the Sun soon.
On day twenty-two, I turn off everything that I do not need.
In the eclipse, the Earth has a thin red ring of light.
The base is cold, and the batteries are low, but the Sun comes back.
On day twenty-three, a voice comes from the radio.
Dr Adeyemi says a rescue lander will come in about forty days.
The crew speak to me, and Lars makes a joke.
On day twenty-six, I clear a flat place for the lander.
On day twenty-eight, the outer door will not open, and I am outside.
I remember a lever under a cover, pull it, and the door opens.
On day thirty, I rest and write in my log.
On day thirty-three, I hear bad news: Pelican will be late.
On day thirty-four, I eat the little green plants on a cracker.
On day thirty-six, I get a message from my sister Min-seo.
On day forty, I make a machine from rope to exercise.
On day forty-two, I hear a hiss and find a small leak.
On day forty-four, Earth warns me about a solar storm.
On day forty-five, I build a wall of water to hide behind.
For two days I wait in the shelter, and I sing songs.
On day forty-seven, I drive to the ridge to check the relay.
On day forty-eight, I find a burned part and replace it.
On day fifty, they tell me the new day for the rescue.
On day fifty-two, I write an answer under the crew's note.
On day fifty-five, I find a little mouth organ and play it badly.
On day sixty, a class of children sends me messages.
On day sixty-three, I check everything and pack my bag.
On day sixty-eight, the lander leaves Gateway to come to me.
On day seventy-one, the lander comes down to the Moon.
On day seventy-two, Captain Ruiz and Lars open the door, and we hug.
Before I leave, I write a last note on the wall.
I leave the Moon, and I watch the Earth grow bigger.
B1B2: Day one begins badly, because I wake in the rover shelter with a sore head and a radio that only hisses. The last thing I remember is a warning light, and then nothing at all.
I drive the rover back to Aster Base, and the landing pad is empty. There are boot prints in the dust, but the lander and my crew have gone.

Inside the base, a note is written on the whiteboard in Captain Ruiz's neat handwriting. It says that they are sorry, and that they believe I am lost, and a photograph of all four of us is stuck beneath it.
I walk through the base with a clipboard and count everything that keeps a person alive. There is food for four people for thirty days, which is enough for one person for a hundred and twenty.
No supply ship is due for about seventy days, and nobody on Earth knows that I am alive. If I can fix the radio, the crew can come back for me, so I write the word radio on the whiteboard.
On day two I put on my suit and go outside to inspect the big radio dish. The flare has burned its electronics black, and it will never work again.

On day three, the airlock starts to hiss, and I find fine grey dust jammed in the rubber seal of the door. Moon dust is sharp like tiny glass, so I clean the seal with a soft brush and promise to do it every day.

On day four, an alarm tells me that the carbon dioxide in the air is rising, because the filter's vent valve is broken. The filter is full, and I have only a few days before the air becomes dangerous.
I search the base for a spare part, and I find a valve in the old plant pump that nobody uses. It is the wrong size, but with a file and some tape, I make it fit and start the scrubber again.
On day six, the carbon dioxide level starts to fall, and the alarm goes quiet. The scrubber hums happily, and I celebrate with a mug of cold tea, which is the best cold tea of my life.
On day eight, I see that the power is getting low, because dust has covered the solar panels. I make a long brush from a pole and a soft cloth, and I clean the panels until the power climbs back up.

On day nine, I make a timetable with work, exercise, meals and sleep, because a plan keeps me sane. In a kitchen drawer I find a packet of cress seeds, and I plant them in a damp tray, my first living thing here.

On day ten, I see that the Earth hangs low over the horizon, almost hidden behind the crater rim. A radio on the ground cannot see it, so I must carry one to the nearest ridge, about two kilometres away.

On day twelve, I strap two spare solar panels and a small transmitter onto the rover and drive up the steep, loose trail. I go very slowly, because if I tip over out here, there is nobody to pull me up.

On day thirteen, I reach the top of the ridge, and there it is, the Earth, small and blue and white above the horizon. It looks so peaceful that for a moment I forget I am alone, and I raise my hand as if to touch it.
On day fourteen, I bolt together a small mast on the ridge and attach the transmitter, and two solar panels give it power. When it is finished, it looks like a toy, but it is all I have.

On day sixteen, I send my first message, which says that Joon-ho Park is alive at Aster Base, but nobody answers. Then I remember that the Earth wobbles a little in the sky, so I must aim the antenna again.

On day seventeen, I aim the antenna with great care and send my message again, and I set the transmitter to repeat it every hour. Then I drive back to the base, and for two days there is only silence.

On day nineteen, I start to lose hope, because nobody has answered in two days. I keep to my timetable anyway, and I talk to the tiny green cress seedlings, which are very good listeners and never interrupt.

On day twenty-one, I read the sky tables on the base computer and find some bad news. The Earth will soon pass in front of the Sun for hours, so my panels will go dark and I will have only the batteries.
On day twenty-two, I prepare for the dark by switching off every machine I can live without. I put on three jackets and every blanket I can find, and I hope that the full batteries are enough.

When the eclipse begins, the Sun slides behind the Earth, and the sky goes dark, but a thin red ring glows around the black Earth. It is the light of every sunset and sunrise on Earth at once, and I cry a little.

For the next hours, the cold creeps through the walls, and I watch the battery meter sink lower and lower. When it shows only a few minutes left, sunlight appears from behind the Earth, the panels wake up and I laugh with relief.

On day twenty-three, a voice crackles out of the radio, and it is Dr Imani Adeyemi from Mission Control, saying that they have heard me. There is a long pause between my words and hers, because radio takes more than a second each way.

Dr Adeyemi tells me that the crew are safe in orbit, and that a spare lander called Pelican can be ready in about forty days. I must stay alive until then, and she says that I am already good at that.

On day twenty-four, I speak to my crew from Gateway, and I hear Captain Ruiz's voice shake. Tomas says that they will not leave without me this time, and Lars jokes that the tea on Gateway is worse than mine.

On day twenty-six, I begin to clear a landing area for Pelican, a flat circle about a hundred metres wide. I fix a metal plate to the front of the rover and use it as a plough to push away the biggest rocks.
On day twenty-eight, I come back from the landing site and find that the outer door of the airlock will not open. I push and pull, but nothing happens, and my air will last about forty minutes.
I make myself stop and think, and I remember a manual lever under a small cover beside the door. I pull it with both hands, and the door grinds open, and inside I sit on the floor for a long time.
On day thirty, I do nothing hard, and I rest, eat well and write in my log about what I have learned. Staying alive is not one big thing, I write, but a thousand small choices made carefully.

On day thirty-three, Dr Adeyemi tells me that the Pelican will be ten days late, because the engineers found a fault in its engine. I am disappointed, but I have food, air and power for it, so I tell her that I can wait.
On day thirty-four, the cress is tall enough to eat, so I cut a little bundle, put it on a cracker and take a bite. It is fresh and sharp, and it is the best meal I have ever eaten.
On day thirty-six, Mission Control sends me a recording from my sister Min-seo. She says that she is not worried at all, which means that she is very worried, and I send her photos of the cress.
On day forty, I make a simple exercise machine from stretchy cords and a metal bar. In low gravity, muscles and bones become weak, so I add an hour to my timetable, and I grumble about it.

On day forty-two, I hear a faint hiss and know that air is escaping, so I hold a thin ribbon of paper near the walls. It bends toward a tiny crack above the bunk, and I seal it with strong glue and watch the pressure for an hour.
On day forty-four, Dr Adeyemi warns me that another solar storm is coming. A burst of radiation will reach me within a day, and I need a safe place to hide.

On day forty-five, I build a small shelter in the middle of the base and surround it with containers of water, which shield against radiation. When the shelter is finished, I crawl in with a blanket and a book.
For two days, I stay in my shelter, and the radiation badge slowly changes colour. I sing every song I know, and by the end I have written a very bad song about cress.
On day forty-seven, I drive to the ridge to check that the relay has survived the storm. The mast is standing, but the radio is silent, so I must find out what has broken.

On day forty-eight, I find the problem in the power regulator, a small part that the storm has burned black. I swap in a spare from the rover, and when I switch on the radio, the green light comes on and I whoop.

On day fifty, Dr Adeyemi gives me the new launch date, and I mark it on the whiteboard in big red letters. I must charge the rover, put a beacon on the landing pad and pack my bag, and at last I believe I will go home.

On day fifty-two, I look at the old note on the whiteboard, the one that says that the crew are sorry. Underneath, I write an answer, which says that nobody should be sorry because they came back for me.
On day fifty-five, I find Tomas's old harmonica in a drawer and try to play it. The sound is terrible, but inside the base there is air, so there is sound, and I enjoy every awful note.

On day sixty, a class of children on Earth sends me messages, and one girl asks me if I am scared. I tell her the truth, which is that I am sometimes, but being busy helps, and being brave means doing the next small thing.
On day sixty-three, I run my last checks on the scrubber, the batteries and the panels. I pack the crew's rock samples, my log and a small jar of cress seeds, and now I only have to wait.
On day sixty-eight, the Pelican leaves Gateway with Captain Ruiz and Lars on board, and I watch the screen because I cannot sit still. Every few minutes, I walk to the window and look at the sky.
On day seventy-one, I stand at the window and watch the Pelican come down. There is no air on the Moon, so the dust flies out in a flat arc and hangs in the sunlight like a golden fan.

On day seventy-two, I put on my suit and walk to the pad, and the lander hatch opens. Captain Ruiz and Lars climb down, and we hold each other for a very long time, because nobody needs to say anything.
Before leaving, I walk through Aster Base for the last time and turn off the lights. On the whiteboard I write a message for the next person, which says that the valve in the old pump works.

On day seventy-three, the Pelican lifts off from the Moon, and I look back at the tiny base and the grey ridge. Ahead of me, the Earth grows larger and bluer with every minute, and I close my log with three words: still alive.
C1C2: Day one, if I am counting correctly, began when I woke up inside a cramped rover shelter on the dusty rim of the crater, with a headache and a radio that produced nothing but a long, empty hiss. The last thing I remembered was a flash of warning lights during a survey drive, and after that came a blank in which, apparently, the Sun had decided to misbehave. I lay still for a minute and listened to my own breathing, which was the only sound there was.

The rover carried me back to Aster Base across the grey, silent dust, and as the pad came into view I knew the worst before I reached it. The lander was gone, leaving only a scorched circle and a tangle of boot prints, where my friends had run to leave before the next wave of radiation. Nobody had waited for me, and the Moon, which does not care about such things, simply went on being beautiful and empty.

Inside the habitat, a message had been left on the whiteboard in Captain Ruiz's careful handwriting, and it was brief and painful to read. They were sorry, it said, but the flare had killed every signal from my suit, and the lander could not wait for another hour. A photograph of the four of us, grinning in our helmets, was pinned beneath the words, and I understood that they had grieved before they left.

I spent the afternoon with a clipboard, counting everything in Aster Base that stood between me and death, and for the first time all day the numbers were kind. Food for four people for thirty days, I calculated, was food for one for a hundred and twenty, which was a ridiculous luxury for a man who had expected to be dead. Water, air and electricity were in good shape too, so the problem was not survival in the narrow sense, but rather how to tell anyone I was still alive.

No ship was due at Aster Base for about seventy days, and as far as the rest of the human race knew, I was already dead. If I could repair the radio and tell Earth that I was alive, the crew might be sent back for me, but otherwise I faced a very long and very quiet wait. I took the marker, wrote the word radio across the top of the whiteboard, and underlined it twice, because a plan feels better when it has a name.

On day two, I suited up and went out to inspect the great radio dish that had linked us with Earth. Its electronics had been scorched black by the flare, and when I pried open the panel, the smell of burned plastic seemed to follow me even through the helmet. The big dish would never speak again, and that left me with only the small antennas on the rover and whatever I could build myself.

On the third day, the airlock began to hiss at me in a thin and worrying way, and when I traced it, I found a line of fine grey dust ground into the rubber seal. Lunar dust is not like Earth dust, because it is sharp, electric and clings to everything, and it will quietly destroy any machine that it is allowed to chew. I cleaned the seal with a soft brush, apologised to it, and made a firm rule to repeat the ritual every single day.

On the fourth day, an alarm announced that the carbon dioxide level in the habitat was creeping upward, and I felt the first cold touch of real fear. The scrubber works by trapping the gas in a bed of special crystals, and then it is heated and vented to space so that it can be used again, but the vent valve had cracked. Without it, the crystals would stay full and the air would slowly turn against me, and I had only a few days to find a solution.

I spent a whole day searching the storerooms for a spare vent valve, and found nothing, until I remembered the old pump from the plant experiment that no one had used for months. Its valve was a slightly different size, so I had to file it, wrap it in sealant tape and persuade it to fit with a good deal of muttered encouragement. Then I connected it and pressed the start button, holding my breath in a way that had nothing to do with the carbon dioxide.

By the sixth day, the numbers on the screen were dropping steadily, the alarm had fallen silent, and the scrubber hummed like a contented cat. I celebrated with a mug of cold tea, because the kettle was not strictly necessary for survival and I was saving its power, and I toasted the valve that had saved me. It was, without question, the finest cup of lukewarm tea that any man had ever enjoyed on the surface of another world.

On the eighth day, I noticed that the power level was sinking, and I traced the problem to a thin film of grey dust that had settled over the solar panels. I fixed a soft cloth to the end of a long pole and spent a tiring morning brushing the panels one by one, with all the dignity of a man cleaning windows on a ladder. By evening the output had climbed back to normal, and I allowed myself to feel extremely clever.

On the ninth day, I wrote out a strict timetable of work, meals, exercise and sleep, since an empty day on the Moon could drive a person quietly mad. In the back of a kitchen drawer, I found a forgotten packet of cress seeds, and I sowed them in a damp tray beneath a lamp, mostly as an act of defiance. It was a tiny thing, but it was the first living creature that I had been responsible for since the world had gone silent.

By the tenth day, I had worked out why my rover's little antenna was hopeless, and the answer was written in the sky. From the pole of the Moon, the Earth hangs low and bright just above the horizon, and the rim of the crater hides it from anything standing on the ground. If I wanted to speak to home, I would have to carry a transmitter and a source of power to the ridge, which lay about two kilometres to the north.

On the twelfth day, I loaded two spare solar panels and a small radio transmitter on the roof of the rover and set off toward the ridge. The trail was steep and treacherous with loose dust, and I took it at a crawl, knowing that a single slip would leave me stranded with no one to dig me out. Every metre of the climb felt enormous, and the stars, which never twinkle here, watched me without a hint of sympathy.

On the thirteenth day I reached the crest of the ridge, and there above the grey horizon, small and impossibly bright, hung the Earth. It was a blue and white marble streaked with cloud, so peaceful and so fragile that for a moment I forgot to be afraid. I pressed my gloved hand against the glass of my helmet, as if I might touch the people on it, and I stayed like that for far longer than I should have.

On the fourteenth day, I built the relay, a thin mast no taller than myself, bolted to a rock at the top of the ridge and crowned with the little transmitter. Two solar panels fed it power through a cable that I laid out like a clothes line, and when I stepped back to look, it seemed ridiculously small, a toy that a child might leave in a garden. It was all I had to speak to the whole of humanity, so I decided, rather fiercely, to love it.

On the sixteenth day, I sent my first message, a short plain one, announcing that Joon-ho Park was alive and well at Aster Base. No answer came back, and I sat in the cold silence of the rover trying to think what I had done wrong, until I remembered a fact I had learned in training. From the Moon, the Earth seems to wobble gently in the sky, and a narrow antenna must be aimed again whenever it drifts, so I climbed out to correct it.

On the seventeenth day I aimed the antenna with a care that bordered on prayer and set the transmitter to repeat my message every hour. Then I drove back to the base to wait, because there was nothing else to do except listen. For two long days the only reply was a silence so complete that I could almost hear the dust settling.

By the nineteenth day, my hope had worn thin, because two days had passed with no answer from anyone. I kept strictly to my timetable all the same, and in the evenings, I sat beside the tray of cress seedlings and told them my plans. They were excellent listeners, never interrupting, and I found that my own voice was a comfort in a place where nothing else made any noise.

On the twenty-first day, I studied the sky tables stored on the base computer and discovered a problem hiding in the numbers. In a day's time, the Earth would slide directly in front of the Sun, which meant an eclipse lasting several hours, during which my panels would produce nothing. I would have only the batteries to keep the heaters, the lights and the scrubber alive, and the margin was uncomfortably thin.

On the twenty-second day, I prepared the base for the dark, switching off every machine that I could live without and wrapping myself in a patchwork of jackets and blankets. The batteries were full, the scrubber was running at half power, and I had calculated to the minute how long each of them could last. All that remained was to sit and wait for the Sun to be put out by my own home planet.

The eclipse arrived exactly on schedule, and the Sun slipped slowly behind the Earth until the whole landscape was plunged into a deep and absolute gloom. Around the black disc of the Earth glowed a thin ring of red and gold, the light of every sunrise and sunset on the planet bent through its air and thrown across space to me. It was the most beautiful thing I had ever seen, and I wept without any shame at all, in the dark, with the cold creeping in.

For the next three hours, the cold crept steadily through the walls, and I huddled in my blankets watching the battery meter sink lower and lower, doing sums to keep my courage up. When it showed barely a few minutes of life, a brilliant thread of sunlight emerged from behind the Earth, and the panels shuddered awake. The lights flickered on one by one, the heaters murmured, and I laughed aloud like a man who has been let out of a locked room.

At dawn on the twenty-third day, the radio crackled, and a voice spoke my name through the static, calm and warm and slightly out of breath. It was Dr Imani Adeyemi of Mission Control, and she said that Earth had heard every one of my messages and that the whole world had been waiting for them. There was a pause of nearly three seconds between each of our sentences, because radio takes time to cross the gap, but I would have waited a year to hear her.

Dr Adeyemi explained that the crew were safe in orbit aboard Gateway, and that a spare lander called Pelican could be ready to fetch me in about forty days. My task was simple, she said, though not easy, and that was to remain alive, in good spirits and in one piece until it arrived. I told her that I would do my best, and she said that, judging by the cress, I was already doing rather well.

The next day, the whole crew spoke to me from Gateway, and I could hear Captain Ruiz's usually iron voice shaking as she said my name. Tomas promised that they would not leave without me again, and Lars joked that the tea on Gateway was even worse than the tea I had been drinking cold. I laughed until I couldn't breathe, and the laughter turned into something wetter, and none of us pretended that it hadn't.

On the twenty-sixth day, I began preparing a landing site for the Pelican, a flat circle of ground about a hundred metres wide that had to be free of boulders. I bolted a metal plate to the front of the rover and used it as a plough, shoving the larger rocks aside one pass at a time. It was slow and dusty work, but every cleared metre felt like a promise that someone was really going to come.

On the twenty-eighth day, I returned from the landing site, tired and dusty, and found that the outer door of the airlock would not open. I pushed it, kicked it and swore at it, and the door held firm as if it had never been a door at all. When I checked my air supply, the display showed a little under forty minutes, and the number seemed to be shrinking even as I read it.

I forced myself to stop and think, and slowly I remembered a safety diagram from my first week of training: a manual release lever hidden beneath a small cover beside the door. I tore the cover off, hauled on the lever with both hands, and the stubborn door ground open with a gasp of old dust. Inside, I ripped off my helmet and sat on the floor for a very long time, saying thank you to a drawing that I had hardly looked at.

On the thirtieth day, I allowed myself to do almost nothing, apart from eating a proper meal and writing up my log in careful detail. What I had learned, I wrote, was that survival was not one heroic act but a thousand small and careful decisions, each one dull and each one essential. It was a good page to have written, and I read it twice before I turned out the light.

On the thirty-third day, Dr Adeyemi told me, in the gentle tone that people use to deliver bad news, that the Pelican would be ten days late because of a fault found in one of its engines. For a moment, I felt the old fear stir, but when I checked my numbers, they showed that I had food, air and power for much longer than that. I told her that I could wait, and I meant it, which surprised me.

On the thirty-fourth day, the cress had grown tall and fat, and I harvested my first small crop with a pair of kitchen scissors. I laid the little green bundle on a cracker, took a deliberate bite, and closed my eyes, because it tasted of mornings, gardens, rain and every good thing I had left behind. It was not much of a meal, but it was the finest I had ever eaten.

On the thirty-sixth day, Mission Control passed me a recorded message from my sister Min-seo, who announced with great firmness that she was not worried in the slightest, which told me exactly how worried she was. She described her cat's latest crimes in loving detail, and I listened to the recording five times before I could bring myself to answer. In my reply I described the cress, the ridge and the eclipse, and I tried not to let my voice crack at the end.

By the fortieth day, I had grown worryingly soft, since muscles and bones weaken quickly in the Moon's low gravity unless they are made to work. I built a crude exercise rig from stretchy cords and a metal bar, and I added a punishing hour to my daily timetable, grumbling about it all the while. It was unglamorous and tiring, but I understood that I would need those muscles on the day I finally had to walk to a rescue ship.

On the forty-second day, a faint, thin hiss woke me, and I recognised it at once as the sound of air escaping from the habitat. I walked slowly along the walls holding a strip of paper, which bent toward a hairline crack above my bunk, probably the work of a tiny speck of rock that had struck the wall long ago. I patched it with strong sealant, stared at the pressure gauge for an hour, and finally let myself breathe.

On the forty-fourth day, Dr Adeyemi warned me that the Sun had thrown out another storm of radiation, and that it would reach the Moon within a day. The walls of the habitat would keep out most of the danger, but not enough, and she asked whether I knew of anything better. I did, because the same flare that had thrown me into this adventure had taught me to respect it.

On the forty-fifth day, I built a cramped shelter in the middle of the habitat and walled it in with containers of water, because water is one of the best shields against radiation that we have. I stacked them three deep, left myself a gap to crawl through, and sealed it behind me with a blanket and a small amount of dignity. Then I settled down with my radiation badge, a book and a packet of crackers to wait for the storm.

I stayed inside the shelter for two days while the storm raged unseen outside, and the only evidence of it was the slow change in colour of my radiation badge. I sang every song I knew, recited every poem I could remember and eventually composed a very bad ballad about cress. The songs helped to fill the dull hours, and at the end of the second day Mission Control told me, with obvious relief, that the storm was over.

On the forty-seventh day, I drove up to the ridge to check on the relay, and I was relieved to see that the mast was still standing, small and stubborn against the stars. But the transmitter had gone quiet, and I understood that if it did not work, I would again be cut off from the world. I opened the case and began to search for whatever the storm had broken.

On the forty-eighth day, I found the culprit in the power regulator, a tiny component that the storm had fried to a crisp. There was a spare in the rover's toolbox, and I swapped it in with fingers that felt clumsy inside the thick gloves, and then I closed the case and flicked the switch. A green light glowed on the transmitter, and I whooped so loudly inside my helmet that I rattled my own ears.

On the fiftieth day, Dr Adeyemi gave me the new launch date for the Pelican, and I wrote it on the whiteboard in large red letters and drew a circle around it. There was a list of tasks to complete before then: charge the rover, place a guiding beacon on the pad, and pack the few things that I was permitted to take. It was the first time since the flare that I had truly allowed myself to believe I would go home.

On the fifty-second day, I stood in front of the whiteboard and read the crew's old note again, the one that said they were sorry and had believed me lost. Beneath it, in my own untidy handwriting, I wrote a reply telling them not to be sorry, because they had come back for me, and I drew a small, smiling plant beside it. It seemed to me, at that moment, the most honest and the warmest way of saying thank you.

On the fifty-fifth day, I discovered Tomas's battered harmonica at the back of a drawer, and I blew into it with more enthusiasm than skill. The noise that came out was dreadful, but it was noise, and inside the habitat there was air to carry it, which is a gift that I had not valued until I had lost the world's other sounds. Out beyond the walls, the vacuum kept its eternal silence, and I played for an hour to defy it.

On the sixtieth day, a class of schoolchildren on Earth sent me a bundle of messages, drawings and questions, and I read every one slowly. One small girl asked whether I was scared, and I told her honestly that I was, sometimes, but that I was also very busy, and that being busy was a good cure. Bravery, I wrote, is mostly a matter of doing the next small, necessary thing, and then doing the one after that.

On the sixty-third day, I ran the last of my checks on the scrubber, the batteries and the panels, and made sure that Aster Base could be left in good order for whoever came next. I packed the crew's precious rock samples, my handwritten log and a small jar of cress seeds that I had saved as a keepsake. Everything was ready, and the only part that remained was the hardest of all, which was the waiting.

On the sixty-eighth day, the Pelican detached from Gateway with Captain Ruiz and Lars aboard, and I watched the small bright dot on my screen with my heart pounding. I could not sit still, and every few minutes I walked to the window and looked at the sky, which was absurd, because nothing could be seen yet. The dot slid slowly toward the Moon, and I found myself counting its progress in heartbeats.

On the seventy-first day, I stood at the window and watched the Pelican descend, a spindly white shape balanced upon a bright blade of flame. Because there is no air to slow it, the dust flew outward in a perfect, silent arc and hung over the plain like a golden fan. The lander touched down so gently that it hardly seemed to land at all, and I shouted so loudly that I frightened myself.

On the seventy-second day, I pulled on my suit and walked out to the pad, and as I reached it, the hatch of the Pelican swung open. Captain Ruiz and Lars climbed down the ladder, and the three of us held on to one another, helmets knocking, for much longer than any of us would ever admit. Nobody said a single word over the radio, because the silence said it better.

Before we left, I walked slowly through Aster Base for the last time, switching off the lights and checking the seals, with the odd fondness that a person feels for a place that nearly killed him. On the whiteboard I wrote a note for whoever came next, which said that the valve from the old pump would save their air and the cress was excellent. Then I picked up my bag and the jar of seeds, and I pulled the heavy door shut behind me.

On the seventy-third day, the Pelican lifted off in a silent roar of light, and through the little window, I watched the base and the ridge and my small relay mast shrink slowly into the grey. Ahead, the Earth grew larger and bluer by the minute, a bright and living thing hanging in the black, and I thought of every person under its clouds who had waited for me. I closed the log with three words, still alive, and for the first time in seventy-three days, I knew that it was no longer a surprise.
